title: A fiber builder's county agreements

blocks.text: A fiber builder plans its network for 2027 to 2029 under agreements with the counties it builds in. The model in `counties.py` has a binary `x[pid, t]` for each project and each year `t` in its `starts`; each project starts at most once (given). A project's `cost` is a tuple: what it spends in its first year of work, its second, and so on, so a project with cost `(300, 200)` started in 2027 spends 300 in 2027 and 200 in 2028. All work ends by 2029. The agreements, in $k:

items: **Minimum.** Each county in `floor` receives at least `floor[c]` over the whole plan.
**Cap over the plan.** Each county in `cap` receives at most `cap[c]` over the whole plan.
**Cap in a year.** For each `(c, y)` in `yearly_cap`, county `c` receives at most `yearly_cap[c, y]` in year `y`.

blocks.text: Write `add_county_rules(model, x, projects, years, floor, cap, yearly_cap)` so that the model allows exactly the plans that keep the three agreements.
The model so far, with $`P`$ the projects, $`T_i`$ project $`i`$'s start years and $`c_{i,k}`$ what it spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($`k = 0, 1, \dots`$):

Name the counties and the projects of each, and write two expressions first: a county's spend in one year, and its spend over the plan. Then write each row with its quantifier and a label, and only then code them.

A county may have no project that spends in some year. Its spend there is a sum over no terms, the number 0 in Python, and MathOpt refuses a row with no variable on either side. Skip such a row, or start the sum from `mathopt.LinearExpression()` (lesson 6.4.1).
The tests fix every `x[pid, t]` through its bounds and ask the solver whether the model accepts the plan, so any correct formulation passes. About twelve lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Project:
    pid: str
    county: str
    cost: tuple[int, ...]
    starts: tuple[int, ...]


def add_county_rules(model: mathopt.Model, x: dict, projects: list[Project], years: tuple[int, ...],
                     floor: dict[str, int], cap: dict[str, int], yearly_cap: dict[tuple[str, int], int]) -> None:
    """Each county's minimum and cap over the plan, and its caps in single years."""
    # TODO: the spend expressions and the three kinds of rows.
    return None


def build(projects: list[Project], years: tuple[int, ...], floor: dict[str, int], cap: dict[str, int],
          yearly_cap: dict[tuple[str, int], int]) -> tuple[mathopt.Model, dict]:
    model = mathopt.Model(name="counties")
    x = {(p.pid, t): model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{p.pid}_{t}") for p in projects for t in p.starts}
    for p in projects:
        model.add_linear_constraint(sum(x[p.pid, t] for t in p.starts) <= 1, name=f"once_{p.pid}")
    add_county_rules(model, x, projects, years, floor, cap, yearly_cap)
    return model, x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    projects = [Project("F1", "Ash", (300, 200), (2027, 2028)), Project("F2", "Ash", (250,), (2027,))]
    model, x = build(projects, (2027, 2028, 2029), {"Ash": 400}, {"Ash": 700}, {("Ash", 2028): 300})
    print(model.get_num_linear_constraints(), "rows")

cases.says: a plan that gives each county its minimum is allowed, and one that leaves a county short is refused
a plan over a county's cap for the plan is refused
a plan over a county's cap for one year is refused
a project's second year of spend counts toward that year's cap
a project's whole cost counts toward its county's minimum, not only its first year

origin.section: A Jurisdiction's Spend Is the Same Sum Over Its Own Projects

concepts: a jurisdiction's limits are rows on the spend of its own projects, over the plan or in one year
